stories.summary:
# Summary

A new brain imaging study found that aging brains don't simply forget memories more weakly; instead, they blend unrelated memories together, creating false connections across different categories (like confusing a scene with an object). The research shows that brain activity patterns associated with accurate memory recall in younger adults actually predict confusion errors in older adults, suggesting their brains retrieve information too broadly rather than replaying specific memories faithfully. This blending phenomenon wasn't fully explained by brain shrinkage or attention differences alone.

stories.summary: The browser's main thread handles nearly all JavaScript execution and screen rendering, making it a bottleneck for performance—when blocked for more than 10-50 milliseconds per frame, it causes noticeable stuttering and input lag. This article explores what the main thread does and presents strategies for optimizing it, either by dividing its workload more efficiently or offloading tasks to other threads like workers or the compositor. Understanding and managing main thread usage becomes critical for interactive websites with heavy data streams and animations, even when network and bundle sizes are already optimized.

stories.title: Intrusive Linked Lists
stories.author: tripdout

topComments.author: el_pollo_diablo
topComments.text: The go a bit further than the article on the advantages of intrusive data structures, taking linked lists as an example: As the article mentions, intrusive data structures naturally lead to one fewer indirection. To do the same with a traditional list (where the list node owns the payload), a different node type is needed for each payload type. This is easy to do with the proper support for monomorphized generics, see C++'s std::list. It is awkward in C, where the implementation has to be macro-generated. C naturally pushes towards an indirection through void *, which makes intrusive lists more attractive. One other advantage of intrusive data structures is the ability to link a payload into several parallel collections without indirections (where traditional collections would require e.g. one collection owning the payloads, and the other collections merely holding non-owning pointers to them). Las but not least, the defining property of intrusive data structures is that they leave the responsibility of allocating the elements to the user. The elements can be allocated on the heap, on the stack, in a global array (like "initholes" in the article), in a special arena, etc. It is even reasonable to use non-uniform allocation strategies; for example, for a circular list, allocate an anchor node on the stack and the other nodes (those embedded in payloads) on the heap.

topComments.author: klps10
topComments.text: I think this article rewrites history and it is unfortunately already cited by the clankers. "Intrusive" is C++ speak. The regular linked lists always had embedded data or a mix of embedded data and pointers to outside data in a C struct.

topComments.author: pclmulqdq
topComments.text: I was surprised to see the main benefit of intrusive linking mentioned as a bit of a side note: The ability to move data around between lists (and within a list) without copying. You also get O(1) removal from the middle of the list, assuming you have a pointer to the object somewhere else. As a result, when you have large state structs and you don't do a lot of list scans, intrusive linking makes things a lot faster than use of packed structures like vectors.

topComments.author: flohofwoe
topComments.text: Hmm interesting, the doubly linked list presented here is missing the elegant 'overlapped list header' trick from AmigaOS (at least that's where I saw it first): E.g. an AmigaOS list node looks conventional, it has two pointers, one to the next node (succ), and one to the previous node (pred): struct Node { struct Node* ln_Succ; struct Node* ln_Pred; }; Most AmigaOS structs embed such a Node struct at the start. ...but the list header has three pointers which basically form two overlapped Node structs: struct List { struct Node* lh_Head; struct Node* lh_Tail; struct Node* lh_TailPred; }; In an empty list, lh_Head points to &lh_Tail, and lh_TailPred points to &lh_Head. The lh_Tail pointer is always null (this is the 'end marker'). In a populated list, lh_Head points to the embedded Node struct of the first list node, and lh_TailPred points to the embedded Node struct of the last list node. The ln_Succ pointer of the last node points to the address of the list header's lh_Tail pointer (...which is always null). That way you only need an existing node pointer to walk forward and backward, or insert or remove a node. When walking the list by following the succ or pred pointers you know you've reached the end when encountering a null pointer. Apparently the Linux-style lists in the article require to know the address of the list header to detect when the end is reached which isn't needed for the Amiga style list (at the cost of an additional 'sentinel null pointer' in the list header). Pretty much all of AmigaOS was held together by such doubly linked lists. (I hope I got that all right, it's been a long time)

stories.summary: This article explains intrusive linked lists, where list nodes are embedded within the data structures themselves rather than stored separately, and describes their advantages in memory efficiency and cache performance. It covers the technical implementation details, including how to navigate embedded lists using pointer arithmetic and the offsetof macro. The article also introduces circular doubly linked lists and explains why Linux extensively uses these data structures for managing processes and other kernel operations.

Nothing downstream of the VIN moves when a module is reflashed, so no registration, history report or dealer system knows what software is actually in a car. stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am on a Skylake-X machine. Here's a very simple loop: %include "events_asm.inc" section .data fmt: db "CYCLES = %lu, RETIRED = %lu", 10, 0 section .text global main extern perf_measure2 kernel: mov rax, 1000000 xor rdi, rdi xor rsi, rsi xor rdx, rdx align 32 .loop: add rdi, rdi sub rsi, rdi and rdx, rdx dec rax jnz .loop ret main: push rbp mov rdi, kernel mov rsi, fmt mov rdx, CYCLES mov rcx, RETIRED call perf_measure2 wrt ..plt pop rbp ret perf_measure2 is a simple helper that uses perf_event_open underneath to sample the two counters and print them. The program itself is meaningless, it only exists to probe CPU behavior. CYCLES is an alias to CPU_CLK_UNHALTED.THREAD_P and RETIRES is an alias to INST_RETIRED.ANY_P. Here are the numbers I am seeing for kernel : CYCLES = 1448789, RETIRED = 5000650 dec and jnz macro-fuse and we're counting in unfused domain with INST_RETIRED.ANY_P, that's why we have ~5M instructions retired in the loop but rest assured we are executing no more than 4 micro-ops per iteration in the loop. With Skylake-X having 4 INT ALUs on p0156, I expected this to be no worse than 1c/iter despite the intra-iteration dependency from add to sub through rdi in the loop. Note that the other 3 ALU instructions are independent, so they can schedule together with a sub from a past iteration. I expected the dynamic scheduler to do this (X.0 here means instruction X, iteration 0): c0: add.0 and.0 dec.0 c1: sub.0 add.1 and.1 dec.1 <--- steady state reached here c2: sub.1 add.2 and.2 dec.2 ... As per my mental model, we are issuing 4 1c micro-op per cycle in the steady state so we should expect to retire 4 instructions every cycle too.
